articles.description: Warm temperatures 6C to 12C above monthly averages expected Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australians in the nation’s south-east are expected to experience the warmest September day in years, with temperatures rising 6C to 12C above average over the weekend. Coastal areas are expected to reach the high 20s while inland regions will extend into the low to mid 30s, as a cold front in Western Australia and a high-pressure system in the Tasman Sea drag warm, dry and sunny weather towards south-eastern Australia, Bureau of Meteorology senior meteorologist Dean Narramore said. articles.title: 2 rare and huge warm-bodied fish called opah caught off Antique
articles.description: ILOILO CITY — Two rare opahs, unusual among fish for their ability to keep their bodies warmer than the surrounding seawater, were caught off Caluya, Antique, on Thursday, Sept. 17. The larger fish weighed about 80 kilos and the other, about 60 kilos. The catch is only the second recorded occurrence of the deep-water fish in Antique, according to licensed fisheries technologist and biodiversity researcher Flord Nicson Calawag. Locally known as “tabas” and also called moonfish, opah are rarely encountered oceanic fish that inhabit open waters and can range into considerable depths. articles.title: The world’s rivers are at breaking point. Can we save them before it is too late?
articles.description: In this week’s newsletter: As the Guardian launches a year-long project, Our Rivers, we take stock of the issues facing waterways around the world Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The nicknames of the world’s biggest rivers give a sense of how we feel about them: “the great river”, “the river that swallows all rivers”, “Mother Ganga” and “Old father Thames”. They feed and water us, and many other animal species. They carry our trade but also give us cool relief on a hot day. They’re nerve endings, elders and sources of comfort, but also of awe and respect. And yet many of the world’s rivers are suffering, hit by multiple environmental challenges. A new report out today from the World Meteorological Organization finds that rivers across the world experienced one of the driest years in more than three decades during 2025.
